[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mastering Object Detection: YOLO vs. Faster R-CNN"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Object detection is a foundational computer vision task that goes beyond image classification. It involves not only identifying what objects are present in an image (classification) but also determining their precise spatial locations (localization using bounding boxes). This tutorial explores two dominant paradigms in object detection: Faster R-CNN (a two-stage detector) and YOLO (You Only Look Once, a single-stage detector)."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding the Paradigms"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Before diving into code, it is crucial to understand the architectural differences between two-stage and single-stage detectors. Two-stage detectors first generate a set of candidate region proposals and then classify each proposal. Single-stage detectors treat object detection as a single regression problem, directly predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities from the entire image in one evaluation."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Faster R-CNN: High accuracy, uses a Region Proposal Network (RPN), traditionally slower inference speeds."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"YOLO: Extremely fast inference, processes the image globally, ideal for real-time video analytics."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Implementing Inference with Ultralytics YOLOv8"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"The YOLO framework has evolved significantly. Below is a Python script using the Ultralytics library to load a pretrained YOLOv8 model and perform inference on an input image."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"from ultralytics import YOLO

# Load a pretrained YOLOv8n model
model = YOLO("yolov8n.pt")

# Run inference on an image source
results = model("https://ultralytics.com/images/bus.jpg")

# Process results
for result in results:
    boxes = result.boxes
    for box in boxes:
        print("Class ID:", int(box.cls[0]))
        print("Bounding Box:", box.xyxy[0].tolist())
        print("Confidence:", float(box.conf[0]))"},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Implementing Inference with Torchvision Faster R-CNN"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"For scenarios requiring high precision where inference latency is less critical, Faster R-CNN implemented in PyTorch's Torchvision library is a robust choice. Here is how to run inference using a pretrained Faster R-CNN model with a ResNet-50 backbone."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"import torch
from torchvision.models.detection import fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn, FasterRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_Weights
from torchvision.transforms import functional as F
from PIL import Image

# Load pretrained weights and model
weights = FasterRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_Weights.DEFAULT
model = fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn(weights=weights, progress=False)
model.eval()

# Load and preprocess image
image = Image.open("bus.jpg")
image_tensor = F.to_tensor(image).unsqueeze(0)

# Perform inference
with torch.no_grad():
    predictions = model(image_tensor)

print("Detected boxes:", predictions[0]["boxes"].shape)"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion and Best Practices"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Choosing between YOLO and Faster R-CNN depends strictly on your project constraints. If you are building a real-time system such as autonomous driving perception or video surveillance, YOLO variants are generally preferred. If you are analyzing static high-resolution imagery where missing small objects is heavily penalized, Faster R-CNN remains an industry standard."}]
